episodes.title: Ben Horowitz: The Fight Over Open Source AI
episodes.summary: Ben Horowitz joins Theo Jaffee and Sofia Puccini to discuss one of the biggest debates in AI today: the future of open-source models. They examine the growing push to restrict open models, why Ben believes open source is critical for security, innovation, and competition, and what happens if a handful of frontier labs come to dominate the AI ecosystem. They also discuss distillation, AI monopolies, China's role in open-source AI, robotics, manufacturing, the economics of frontier models, and why Ben believes the AI market is still in its earliest stages. The conversation closes with a look at AI-generated art, creativity, and whether new tools will spark the next cultural renaissance. episodes.title: Dan Harris: Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics [From the Archive]
episodes.summary: Episode Description: This is a From the Archive episode with Dan Harris. Dan Harris returns to the show for a wide-ranging conversation about meditation without the incense, jargon, or grandiose promises. James begins with Dan’s story: his work at ABC News, his public panic attack, his substance abuse, his reporting from war zones, and the recovery path that led him to meditation. Dan’s first book, 10% Happier , made the case that meditation could be useful even for skeptics, strivers, journalists, and people who do not identify with traditional spirituality. This episode focuses on the next step: how to actually start. Dan’s book Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics , written with meditation teacher Jeff Warren and Carlye Adler, tries to remove the usual excuses. You do not need to sit for an hour. You do not need a cushion. You do not need to clear your mind. You do not need to become a different person. You can start with one minute. James and Dan discuss the difference between useful self-reflection and useless rumination, why ambition and meditation are not opposites, and why mindfulness is really the ability to see what is happening in your head without automatically believing it or acting on it. They also get into the science. Dan is careful not to oversell it, but he explains why early research suggests meditation may affect attention, stress, compassion, self-awareness, and the brain’s capacity to change. James adds that the most important experiment is often the simplest one: try it for yourself and see whether your life is better in a month. The emotional center of the conversation is Dan’s relationship with his wife, Bianca. Dan describes how meditation helped him become less self-centered and more available, while Bianca found her own version of practice through Jeff Warren’s “Taking Back Lazy” approach. Her practice began inside real life: lying in the dark while putting their son to bed. The episode then expands into money, news, politics, and productivity. James argues that meditation can improve financial outcomes indirectly by freeing energy, reducing useless thought loops, increasing creativity, and making a person more useful to others. Dan talks about varied news diets, tribalism, and why mindfulness can help people disagree without becoming consumed by antagonism. The result is a practical archive conversation about mental training, not mystical transformation. Meditation will not solve everything. It may not make you 100% happier. But it can help you become 10% less reactive, 10% less self-absorbed, 10% more aware, and 10% more capable of dealing with the life you already have. Editorial Note: This is a From the Archive episode. References to Dan’s ABC role, the original 10% Happier app, user counts, current events, and the release timing of Meditation for Fidgety Skeptics reflect the original recording period. Dan’s current official site now directs listeners to his books, podcast, newsletter, and meditation app/community. The original app world has evolved since this archive conversation. What You’ll Learn: Why Dan Harris became a meditation advocate after his on-air panic attack. Why meditation does not require mystical language, spiritual identity, or long sessions. How mindfulness helps separate awareness from thinking. Why ambition and meditation can coexist. How meditation can reduce useless rumination without eliminating useful self-correction. Why Dan describes self-centeredness as a source of suffering. How “friendliness” can change the way you relate to anger, distraction, and failure during meditation. Why one minute of practice can be enough to start. How Jeff Warren helped Dan’s wife Bianca find a meditation practice that fit her real life. Why meditation can improve relationships by making people less owned by their own stress. How meditation may relate to money, creativity, and better decision-making.
